#4097. GTA 6 has a smell reaction system, which immediately joins Red Dead Redemption 2's dynamically shrinking horse balls on Rockstar's list of immersive symbols of excess

Florida of course being full of smelly smells that smell...smelly

Any reminder of Red Dead Redemption 2's temperature sensitive horse testicles brings a smile to my face. In truth, I can't say I've ever zoomed in close enough to properly take in the spectacle of Arthur Morgan's mount having its nuts dynamically expand and contract based on whether he's riding through snowy mountains or across baking plains, but I do always get a kick out of knowing such a thing's happening as I play. To this point, the horse balls have been the most infamous or meme-worthy example of Rockstar's obsession with going all-in on realistic detail to an arguably unnecessary degree, one that borders on overindulgence which players could conceivably never notice if they weren't expressly told about it.

That philosophy's gone nowhere, so GTA 6 was always going to have a feature that'd become as much of a metaphor for excess as those beloved balls. It may well be the smell reaction system revealed in Edge's long read on the game.

According to this latest rundown of things in GTA 6 and how they were made, Rockstar devs at one point had to make a character react to a not nice smell for a specific bit of "explorable content" stuffed into the game. Cool. One person scrunching their face up to show things are getting stinky in one minigame or mission. Leave it at that.

They reportedly did not leave it at that, later going back to flesh out this one smell reaction into a broader system which other locations to inspire various degrees of face-scrunching by protagonists Lucia and Jason. Cue, in the demo of the game in action which Rockstar gave Edge, Jason walking into a house and starting to act like someone who's just walked into a shower-averse teenager's bedroom during a heatwave despite that not having been set up as part of a deliberately crafted encounter. It's horse ball-esque dynamic systems playing off each other, and voila, a man going eewwwwwwwwwwwww.

Would GTA 6 be any worse off if, as in previous entries, you weren't being shown as expressly which places the crim whose boots you're sharing finds a bit too pongy for their liking? Almost certainly not, but hey, when you've decided your business is taking the detail to levels other games could only dream of having the budget for, getting to the point where you're adding a fiftieth layer of icing to a cake so packed to the gills with different tastes and flourishes that your guests will struggle to appreciate or even notice them all unless you painstakingly point out each one is sort of inevitable.

Another layer of gold wrap on the Bugatti, another brick made of diamonds in a wall projected to be the most lucrative of all time, another farty stench in a room already drowning in foul aromas. It's beautiful in the perverse sort of way that I imagine the Palace of Versailles was to anyone who wandered its gilded halls just prior to the French revolution. To be clear, this isn't any sort of slight on the devs who'll no doubt have worked hard to bring this system and others in GTA 6 to life, a number of whom have a recoginition vote on their unionisation efforts coming up next month.

From a player perspective, one can only hope that by the time GTA 6 hits PC, the RAM crisis has led hardware makers to invest heavily in smellivision tech, so that players around the world can drink in the guffs causing their butt naked on-screen analogue's eyes to water or revel in the stink caused by hitting someone with a bag of dog shit. Forget AI bollocks, this is the future, I scream as I retch into a toilet bowl while some funky tunes from Justice play in the background.

#4096. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 intro cinematic is "not intended to reference or trivialise" real-world South Korean crowd crush, Activision say amid reported backlash

Update: Activision reportedly confirm footage will be removed in November Modern Warfare 4 update

Update: The BBC report that Activision have issued a statement apologising to the victims of the Itaewon crowd crush and confirmed that the news footage from the disaster in Modern Warfare 4's intro cinematic will be removed. An update coming to the shooter on November 12th will do the deed.

The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association have welcomed Activision's decision to pull the footage, according to the BBC, but also said they hadn't received a direct apology from the Call of Duty publishers.

The intro cinematic of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, this year's Activision mil-shooter, has reportedly caused controversy in South Korea due to the use of some real world news footage from a 2022 crowd crush in Seoul's Itaewon district which killed around 150 people. Activision have now issued a response to the situation, in which they state the intro is "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy".

Korean site SBS News have reported on the backlash Modern Warfare 4's opening cinematic has caused in the country. Their story - which it's worth noting has been translated into English by AI, and thus is acknowledged as potentially containing errors - claimed that the shooter's intro features three seconds of real-world broadcast footage showing a emergency workers performing CPR on a collapsed person during the Itaewon crowd crush's aftermath.

The crush saw a crowd of people become trapped in a narrow alleyway during Halloween weekend celebrations in the South Korean capital, with between 150 and 160 people dying as a result of becoming so tightly packed together that some couldn't breathe. According to the report, groups and bodies in Korea including an association representing families who suffered bereavements in the crush have called for Activision to remove the footage from Modern Warfare 4's intro.

Approached for comment by RPS, Activision issued the following statement on the situation:

Modern Warfare 4's campaign is built around a North Korean invasion of South Korea.

#4095. Can the SideWinder Game Pad, Microsoft's first game controller, work on modern PCs? I bought three of them to find out

The past and fiddly present of the Xbox controller's ancestor

1996 gave us two incredible gifts. The first was me. The second, arguably more impactful on the course of human civilisation, was the Microsoft SideWinder Game Pad 1.0.

Chances are you might not have heard of the SideWinder brand. Launched in 1995 with the 3D Pro and Standard joysticks, the hardware family would eventually comprise gamepads, racing wheels, a game voice device to talk with friends and vocally control your game, and a massive mouse with more buttons than my nana’s vest. A genuinely cool collection of peripherals.

However, and perhaps prophetic of how they would eventually set about dismantling a gaming industry they had helped built, Microsoft shuttered the SideWinder brand in 2003, supposedly due to poor sales. An especially funny comment, in hindsight, came from Microsoft Canada’s then marketing manager, Kim McWhinnie:

"While SideWinder devices are very popular, the majority of PC games today are built for a mouse and keyboard interface.”

Well before the yacht-printing success of the Steam Deck and handheld PC gaming, a significant chunk of PC players have long preferred the feel and functionality of a controller. Although the SideWinder name enjoyed a brief resurrection in 2007 with the release of the SideWinder Mouse, and later the SideWinder X6 and X4 keyboards, the gamepad side of the brand would never again see another product, with Microsoft instead opting for PC-compatible versions of their Xbox controllers.

Which bring us to 2026. While making my weekly car boot excursion, the fates conspired to bring me and the SideWinder Game Pad 1.0 together, in the form of a nice old lady asking for 2 euros. Bonafide hardware history, for that little cash? I was sold, and determined to see how a controller from the 90s might stand up to PCs and games of the 21st century.

Sadly, the initial feel of the controller isn’t great. The shell is cut from cheap plastic that sits awkwardly in my hands. Rather than a thumbstick, the controller boasts this odd circular D-Pad that allows for eight directional movement, though the diagonals are notably harder to press. The triggers give a nice clicking sound, but they feel far too thin to enjoy pushing down. The buttons are fine, though the press is much too soft for my thumb-tastes.

The controller does appear to have built with the idea of 'serious gaming' in mind. For instance, the pad comes bundled with software allowing for the creation of macros that can then be deployed at the push of the big M on the controller. Other interesting details include the early design choices that would eventually be mimicked on the first Xbox controller, the "Duke". The omni-directional D-Pad and the triple button rows make their debut here, though the size of the controller is much more in line with the later "Controller S" model, which shed much of the Duke’s girth.

The SideWinder also came with a rather neat 'pass through' port, allowing owners to connect additional SideWinder controllers through the initial controller, daisy chaining up to a total of four. Sadly, I lacked the friends necessary to examine this aspect, so you’ll have to make do with the purely imaginary scenario of securing victory by pulling on your controller hard enough to yank everyone else’s to the ground. Which, if nothing else, shows Microsoft really understood their target audience.

There's no denying the power of old controllers to provoke fond memories in the handler, nor their continued popularity in the modern day - as evident in Nintendo's production of imitation Gamecube and NES pads for the Switch 2. With growing preferences for emulation in the face of bankrupting retro game prices, many either go for custom controllers with modern functionality, or original peripherals connected via adapters, in order to preserve as much of the original experience as possible. But can the same be said for the SideWinder?

While I tracked down an old TV ad for the controller, my trawling of numerous old gaming magazines was less fruitful. I did come across a glowing review from the November 1996 issue of PC Zone by Dave Mathelson, praising the "two clever underneath buttons" (triggers were, indeed, a novelty at the time) and describing the handles as "horns" and the general design, more concerning, as "sexy". The verdict was almost entirely positive, praising both the feel and the ability to create custom control schemes for each of your games. Yet, I feel this line perhaps betrays the controller's struggles:

"While there are plenty of pads now available for the PC, the number of joysticks on the market didn't stop Microsoft from releasing one..."

As much as I find the SideWinder interesting, I'd argue it's more generic-looking than sexy. The late 90s/early 00s gave us attitude, explosions, and impractical designs you could only get by locking up a bunch of coked-up mandrills with CAD modelling software. An era ruled by the SpaceOrb 360 and the Fragmaster, the kind of creations birthed by an out-of-touch executive demanding kung-fu grip. Even Microsoft's own SideWinder Strategic Commander, an early attempt at an RTS mouse, had that strangeness sauce.

By comparison, the SideWinder Game Pad cuts a very subtle figure. There’s a seriousness to it. Still playful, as we are dealing with gaming. The nerd equivalent of dressing up in a new suit but leaving the top button undone. It feels like they were going for something more professional. The macro feature and the ability to customise your controller scheme for each game accentuate this point further, while also showcasing a design ethos Microsoft have long since abandoned: trusting consumers with the product you sold them.

Yet this also means it doesn’t stand out. I think Microsoft must have realised this at some point, as later additions to the SideWinder brand are more distinct, both visually and functionally. The Force Feedback Pro went on to sell over a million units, but the Game Pad hardly gets a mention in the news archives. For every Reddit post or TikTok short or LGR Review on weird and wonderful tech, the bland 1.0 is memory-holed even deeper.

Then, of course, there’s one other serious issue that keeps the SideWinder buried in the cable bin of yesterday: modern compatability.

As you can imagine, these things aren’t exactly easy to get working on a present-day PC.

My desktop, despite being a little dated itself, lacked the necessary connections to test the SideWinder. My motherboard still boasts old-school PS2 connectors for keyboard and mouse, but couldn’t spare a thought for more specialised retro gear. Granted, it’s not hard to see why. The controller (and a lot of the tech from the era) makes use of a 15-pin game port connector, appearing first on dedicated PCI cards, then later sound cards and eventually motherboards. These would eventually be phased out as USB became the go-to connector for personal computers, and while game port-to-USB adapters do exist, and even come bundled with later SideWinder products, procuring one today is surprisingly difficult.

So I went for the next best thing: a sound card from the 90s. A Creative Sound Blaster Live, torn from some ancient machine to grace me with the soft beauty of 16-bit audio and the game port’s connective tissue. I then quickly discovered that the card wasn’t compatible with my motherboard. Growing desperate as I battled both a looming deadline and my partner’s concern at the growing horde of retro tech, I managed to find someone selling two more SideWinders AND the game port-to-USB adapter. I snapped them up, plugged the adapter into my system, aaaaaand...

Nothing. The computer just couldn’t find it.

I’m saddened to admit I still attempted to get the blasted thing working long after this, eventually culminating in injuring myself while attempting to plant the sound card in an older machine. Taking this as a sign from the tech gods that I was not truly worthy of enjoying this artifact, I instead settled for a slightly newer (albeit still ancient) SideWinder Plug and Play. This came with USB out of the box, at the cost of fewer buttons and even less individuality, but I felt it would serve to at least give you some idea of how a SideWinder controller plays. Rest assured that if you think this damages the integrity of this retrospective, there is no one more ashamed than myself.

Prior to writing the article, I had a chat with my dad regarding the SideWinder Game Pad. He couldn’t stop gushing about it, saying how it was one of his favourite controllers back in the day. Unlike with Father Christmas, it appears my dad was telling the truth. The Plug and Play was genuinely fun to use, though perhaps not for the reasons my dad would expect.

I immediately fired up a multiplayer lobby of Titanfall 2, an FPS defined by its intricate movement systems, and proceeded to patiently stroll down the city streets, gaze locked forward. I could neither sprint nor turn the camera. In addition, incomplete control mapping also meant I couldn’t even shoot. I nearly fell out of my chair laughing as I was absolutely and immediately demolished.

I gave the original, 1993 Doom a whirl next, though again faced the issue of needing to dual wield with my PC mouse to rotate the camera for effective demon slaying. I ended up crab-walking into rooms, running back out, and letting the enemies funnel into my view. So somewhat more successful here.

Continuing my testing through retro and modern alike, I unleashed eco justice with Cloud in the original Final Fantasy VII, went bust in a round of Balatro, and tended to my farm in Stardew Valley. The SideWinder held up in all of them. I also gave some upcoming indie demos a whirl, successfully battling a demonic incursion in Entropy but tragically getting torn apart by bugs in The Last Exterminator.

Overall, so long as your game doesn’t require too many inputs (and also ideally takes place entirely within a straight hallway), the controller works great. My verdict? Ideal for Deep Space Corridor.

I'm sure that the SideWinder Game Pad 1.0 can be made to work with modern systems. Given enough time and a few more blows to my bank account, I could either fit my computer with the correct hardware, or hack together a game port adapter with an Arduino board.

I don’t intend to give up, but it’s also a pain point that’s going to be too much for a lot of people. Tech continues to hurtle forward, abandoning anything deemed inefficient for the world of tomorrow, with little care for ensuring compatabiltiy with the successes of yesterday. Sony already showed as much with their promise/threat to ditch physical games media. Do you think Microsoft are going to care about a controller that Asha Sharma has probably never heard of, much less used?

The truth of the matter is that, as foundational as the tech is, the SideWinder Game Pad was just an early casualty in an arms race that has slowly stripped uniqueness, choice, and especially this past year, affordability from players. Give it another decade, and if the tech overlords have their way, we’ll likely be renting our machines, streaming our games, and paying per hour for the privilege of using a controller.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I’m going to enjoy my four SideWinders while I still can.

#4094. Atmosfar is a giddy aerial exploration game after the heart of No Man's Sky, but I'm already trying to escape it

Oh hi there! Why yes, I am free to chat. Please excuse the wind noise, I'm currently tumbling to my doom in Atmosfar, after getting lost in a cloud bank and exhausting my fuel. This kind of thing happens to me regularly in Atmosfar - an open world survival game that plays out across clusters of floating islands, with players scooting about in adorable, propellor-powered airships.

Many of the islands are quite large, with proper landing pads and bases set up by NPC scavengers. Many of them teem with non-human life: rainforests full of nectar droplets and carnivorous plants, meadows of ponderous honking lizards, and mossy grottos where you'll find caches of batteries and possibly get eaten by mantids. It's important to make the most of these larger islands, gathering materials for crafting at your deployable campsite (which straps pleasingly to the back of your whirring fly-mobile). It's particularly important to mine hydrogen crystals you can refine into fuel.

None of that's for me, though! I am a true spirit of the sky. The only fuel I need is my imagination. The only objective marker I acknowledge is the omnidirectional Call to Adventure. Besides, when you do run out of fuel in Atmosfar, you're actually unlocking two exciting minigames. The first consists of leaping from the cockpit and vainly trying to jetpack to the nearest walkable surface. The second consists of racing to overtake your plummeting airship and re-enter the cockpit before you smash into any islands beneath. I'm playing that second minigame right now. Come to papa, my beautiful turboprop son! Ah, balls.

Atmosfar is out in Steam early access today, with plans to stay in early access for at least nine months. I think it has some juice, though I am admittedly already trying to play it against the grain - and at times, trying to do things its technology doesn't quite allow.

It casts you as an interplanetary pioneer who, due to some minor infraction, has been locked up in a factory: a dreary opening area with some corpo-satire elements, from which you are soon liberated by an electrical storm. Busting past the sentry drones, you scramble down a cliffside and discover your very first Wasp hovercar. From there, you have more or less free rein of the game's opening biome, though there's a critical path of tutorials and NPC encounters you'll want to follow for the sake of unlocks, like the jetpack.

The scattered islands do a fair job of luring you from your HUD objectives (the HUD itself is a bit murky, in any case – I struggled to make connections between waypoints and quests in my journal). Even if there's nothing to capital-i Interact with, it's a pleasure to alight on some drifting gobbet of soil and flowers, peer into the crevices, and maybe take a few photos of distant astral mountains.

The searing emptiness all around makes the design of each island feel more precise and careful, gift-wrapped for the player. I find that I'm most interested in the tinier islands, the ones that were presumably a secondary consideration for developers Apog Labs, and maybe handed off to a junior staffer. I gaze at a random grass tuft and try to guess how much ingenuity went into the placement of something many pilots will totally ignore.

I'm already chafing against the survival systems a bit, however. Based on a couple of hours of cloudsteading, Atmosfar's core ingredients aren't particularly novel or involving. There's no tree-chopping, thank god, but you will spend many moments pointing your extractor at a nugget of glowing resourcegook, splitting it into plastic sheets and steel girders and so forth.

Many of the opening missions involve toing and froing between deposits and your airship or camp. It's humdrum stuff. The game's non-player scavengers seem like quest-givers first, characters second. Your inventory size is limited, to begin with. Deeper in, there's the opportunity to construct a huge airbase, the Cloud Cruiser, which I'm really hoping doesn't need refuelling. Although it would be a great joke to accidentally drop one with several co-op buds inside.

I've spent most of my two hours in Atmosfar in headlong retreat from the tutorial quests, trying to reach places I sense I'm not supposed to, without paying my dues to the crafting system. This includes both the ruddier, volcanic areas higher up, which I do believe I can reach, if I bother to refine enough fuel. But I'm more captivated, right now, by what lies beneath.

During a nighttime mission to gather eggs for some outpost chef, I gave into curiosity and aimed my Wasp straight down, spiralling past lonely stalactites with no creature population, into a swirling turquoise abyss full of bare, indistinct rock. As I descended, the game's tech began to creak and fizzle, as though strained by increasing gravity. My ride's exhaust condensed and flattened into glitchy flakes.

I ignored the simulation's protests, holding my course like Ahab aiming a harpoon at Moby Dick's kisser, till a "leaving mission area" reset timer yanked me up short. I ascended to just above the cut-off point, and gawped at the horizon. A juddering white ring enclosed the world, surrounded by wrinkled LIDAR pulses that made me think of thoughts coursing through brain tissue.

Now, this was an adventure. I flapped around a bit, battling turbulence, and managed to land on one of the weirdly unadorned, formless boulders. Who made this? Some procedural generation system, or did somebody actually have to 'hand-craft' these places that are probably not for serious human inquiry or habitation? I shot a few flares over the side and tried to deploy my campsite, but there was too little space on the boulder. Then the sun rose, slowly staining the milky blue fastness pink, and revealing the crisper silhouettes of the properly designed and navigable islands high above.

That last screenshot is my favourite so far - the rosy, rugged beauty of Atmosfar and the bizarre quirks of its technology reaching a strangely persuasive accord. There's only one issue: I've run out of fuel again. I guess I could yeet myself into the void and reset to the nearest landing pad, but that doesn't feel like something a true Spirit of the Sky would do. I guess I'll have to enlist another RPS scribe as a co-op partner and have them come fetch me. Perhaps they can complete the tutorials first and rock up in one of those Cloud Cruiser things. In the meantime, you can get your fill of Atmosfaring via Steam.

#4093. Don't worry, GTA 6's cars can drive for ages before their fuel tanks need refilling, leaving me wondering why this motor management's been added at all

Right, before you groan too hard, I promise that after I write this I'll take a break of indeterminate length from writing articles which amount to wondering aloud why a thing that's in GTA 6 is in GTA 6. Cars which need refuelling. It's not an addition there'd not been any hint was coming before today, as with the smell reaction system, leaks having hinted at fuel management all the way back in August.

Since that point, it's been confirmed as in the version of the game Rockstar will be shipping to consoles (boo) next month and PC at some point after that. Edge's GTA 6 long read notes the existence of fuel gauges and engine health readouts, but it also caveats them in what seems an insistence from Rockstar that the first of these features isn't designed to make filling up something the player necessarily has to do often or spend much time on when they do.

GTA 6's cars, according to Edge, can drive vast distances before they reach the point of running low on fuel, while refuelling is something you can do in quick and fuss-free fashion. On one hand, having cars that can barely drive three streets without sputtering to a halt and making the gas station experience a clunky chore that takes ages clearly would've both been terrible moves.

However, the fact the system's lenience is being emphasised has me wondering why it was worth adding at all. To be fair, Edge do outline that the variable amounts of gas in tanks does work with other new mechanics to add more unpredictability to crime sprees and rewards taking a bit more time to prepare a battle plan for robberies. If there's a chance that random ride you'd usually nick from an NPC on running out into the street with your loot might be running on fumes that won't get you through the ensuing police chase, that makes having proper getaway arrangements made prior to the stick-up more important. Then again, it seems any weapons your character's not got room to carry at any time are stored in their car's trunk in GTA 6 - rather than just shoved in pockets that can somehow fit an RPG - so always bringing your own wheels along on a job might be a no-brainer regardless.

All that in mind, this fuel management feels to me like it might suffer a fate similar to vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker's time mechanics. If you've not played Dawnwalker - you should, here's my review - its devs Rebel Wolves based their story around giving the player 30 days and nights in which to find a way to save their family, lest mysterious consequences occur. Cue some folks feeling put off by the idea their adventuring would be restricted by any sort of time constraints, others concluding that the timer was too lenient to fulfil its role of focusing them on getting their task done in suitably rapid fashion, and people like me feeling like they had about the right amount of days left by the time they were in position to launch one of the game's final missions.

Managing fuel in games, especially ones in which people are used to being able to just get in a car and drive for as long as they fancy, tends to be similarly polarising. I can see some GTA 6 players raging against the idea that they've ever got to stop rampaging or partying to do something as mundane as fill up. I can see others being disappointed that, in trying to ensure that first group aren't put off, Rockstar have diluted the mechanic to the point it's not forcing players to fill up at a cadence that feels realistic in the way features like this are supposed to at their best. Many may end up thinking an ideal compromise has been reached. This can be the case with any feature in any game to a degree and all of us should at least try a game in the form its devs envisioned before resorting to moaning for more options or seeking out mods.

Though, as the driving games out there already prove, when it comes to fuel simulation it's usually best for studios to go all-in on committing to the mechanic if they're going to implement it, rather than trying to occupy a mushy middle ground. In full-blown sims like either of SCS's truck sims, SnowRunner, and iRacing, it's an obvious inclusion because the central appeal of those games lies in mirroring motoring in realistic detail. In open-world arcade racers like Forza Horizon, Need For Speed, and Burnout, it's usually cast aside as the sort of thing that'd be more of an annoying limitation than a welcome wrinkle, with filling stations that do appear often limited to dishing out nitrous or boost for extra speed instead.

Up until now, GTA's always fallen on the latter side of the fence and honestly seemed at home there. It's been an action-filled crime romp, not a life sim, and its cars have been designed to best suit that identity. With 6, though, Rockstar are skewing harder into the latter, as they did with Red Dead Redemption 2. RDR2's beloved, the majority of players could well end up adjusting to or appreciating this extra layer of thinking they'll have to do whenever they fire up their wheels. In my estimation, however, fuel management's the biggest risk Rockstar are taking with any of their new additions. The series is called Grand Theft Auto, after all. You're only messing with a wheeled aspect of it so central that they're right there in the name.

#4091. Queen's Domain is a brilliant King's Field-alike RPG that forces you to walk so you can learn to fly

I would also have accepted "Prince's Place" or "Baron's Turf"

FromSoftware's elderly King's Field games aren't really celebrated for their feeling of agility. They are glorious first-person trudgefests, a treacle-thick waltz of swinging and spellcraft, with players wobbling in and out of attack range like British men who aren't sure whether the other man wants a hug. Unlike in the later Dark Souls action-RPGs, to which King's Field owes some of its retrospective popularity, there's no dodge-roll to grease the wheels.

Out this week on Steam, Queen's Domain is often as ponderous as King's Field, but it's also an exercise in steady, triumphant acceleration. Ultimately, it wants you to fly. To this end, it equips you - well, once you've boshed a huge skeleton sentinel - with a fancy windblade that lets you perform an aerial dash, speeding your manouevres while allowing you to reach new areas.

You'll find socketable gems that extend the dash, gradually bringing offshore islands and collapsed castle parapets within reach. I'm around four hours into Queen's Domain, and right now, the overall objective is tricking out that enchanted blade: heading down one leg of a marvellous, knotty world, retrieving a gem, and returning along another path, while keeping an eye out for nooks and platforms that once seemed like cordoned-off backdrop.

While an obvious quick-select default, the windblade doesn't make the 50 or so other weapons in the game obsolete, partly because enemies are distinguished by damage type: skellingtons are tougher against swords, while spears tend to bounce off malformed rodent ladybugs. All the weapons level up with use, and all of them have special abilities: the first spear you acquire has a retreating stab, useful against grasshopper chickens with lunging kicks, while the basic wooden club has a pounce move, skipping the lengthy swinging animation that is the weapon's major disadvantage.

For all these flourishes, combat is often as reassuringly stodgy as I remember King's Field being on the early PlayStation consoles. The pace is set by the need to charge your attacks, holding the button till the wind-up consumes your whole stamina bar; spamming blows is much less efficient.

350 words in, and I haven't mentioned the standout attraction in Queen's Domain – the landscape itself, an absurdly lovely expanse of mossy arches, chopped pillars and racked tombs that evokes Shadow of the Colossus and Vagrant Story as much as it does FromSoftware. It's a beautiful place, a haunting recovery of PS2 aesthetics that runs comfortably on integrated graphics. Or at least, it's beautiful until you start screwing around with focal length and lurid filters in the Photo Mode (see below).

The archipelago's interwoven paths are structured around save crystals where you can rest at the price of respawning enemies, but unlike in Souls, enemies eventually respawn of their own accord, appearing in different combinations as you pass certain milestones.

If this last wrinkle creates more potential for ambush, you can shape encounters using your secondary weapons, beginning with a belt of throwing daggers hanging from a shipwreck. I specify the location because embarrassingly, I managed to overlook them for the first hour – in general, Queen's Domain doesn't highlight collectible objects as flagrantly as certain recent blockbusters.

You get an endless supply of daggers, governed by a cooldown. The best thing about them initially is that you can use them to murder the highly annoying laser eyeballs that deck the tree trunks, often zapping you in the back while you're battling something else. Beyond that, you'll use them to bait individuals away from mobs, luring them towards killzones with plenty of strafing room, or getting them jammed behind monoliths so that you can bop their noggins at leisure.

I've got over 30 hours of Queen's Domain left to burn, according to devs Freshly Baked. Unlike with a lot of the non-review games I've dipped into this year, I feel like I might actually go the distance. More thoughts to follow, possibly! If you're new to King's Fieldalikes, you may find this stifling and frustrating at first. Even if you do know your King's Fields, you'll likely perish a lot. But hopefully, the landscape's magnificence and the increasing swagger of the combat system will get you over the hump. The game launches tomorrow, and there's still a demo on Steam as of writing.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is finally out in the wild a good 28 years after Nintendo's original gem dropped back in 1998, and is already proving to be the highest-rated game of 2026 thus far.

Sure, it's a remake, but it slots in nicely between all the other new games – and it's still just as valuable, too, as Nintendo senior vice president of product development and publishing Nate Bihldorff explains to Polygon. "I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest. There are fans of every single IP that we have out there," as he says. Remakes are very welcome to those fans, to say the least.

"Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there's also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time" – and that's evident in how well the remake is doing already, if you ask me. It made Metacritic's top 30 games of all time within a day, proving that the community is very much happy to enjoy remakes as it is entirely fresh titles.

Longtime Legend of Zelda fans aren't the only people immersing themselves in Nintendo's revamped spin on Hyrule, either. As Bihldorff states, "It's also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on." A quick look at social media proves his assertion here right.

Remakes don't just cater to old fans, but they help introduce countless more to long-standing franchises and series like The Legend of Zelda. They certainly don't take away from new releases, either – every fellow Zelda stan I know is on the edge of their seat waiting for more announcements from Nintendo, especially after the likes of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. I don't see that changing, ever.

While you're here, be sure to read our The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review. You can also check out our Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock live blog if you want to grab one of Nintendo's highly-sought-after new consoles.

#4088. Celeste and TowerFall have been removed from the Xbox store in a move to "support the BDS boycott" against Microsoft

This follows fellow indie dev House House announcing Big Walk will not be coming to Xbox

It's a good day to love Celeste! Earlier today it was discovered that Celeste had been removed from the Xbox Store while it remained on the PlayStation and Nintendo digital storefronts. Now, as shared by the game's co-creator Maddy Thorson, it's been confirmed that both Celeste and TowerFall were removed from store expressly in support of the BDS called boycott against Xbox over Microsoft providing support to the Israeli military as it enacts its genocide of the Palestinian people.

A larger statement hasn't been made by other Celeste developers or Thorson's current studio EXOK Games, but the larger more important point is that the games are no longer available for purchase on the Xbox Store. Earlier this month, House House, developer of one of the biggest indies of the year Big Walk, also shared their own support for the BDS movement and Microsoft boycott announcement by announcing their (quite excellent) social puzzle game will not be launching on Xbox for the foreseeable future. Developer Origame Digital also made an incredibly potent statement denouncing the genocide in their latest game, Penguin's Colony.

For those who’re asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on XBox. We did this to support the BDS boycott

For those not in the know, BDS called for the boycott of Microsoft and Xbox games and hardware last year over the tech company providing AI software to the Israeli military which was used specifically to target Palestinian civilians; Microsoft have even confirmed that they were providing this software. They remain on the BDS boycott list due to the fact they continue to provide the Israeli military with other services such as email and file management systems, as well as for "combat and intelligence activities."

The actions of EXOK Games, House House and Origame Digital come at a time of a growing pushback against Xbox over Microsoft's support of the military movement, in part from No Games for Genocide, an organisation made up of developers and industry practitioners (disclaimer: I myself am an organiser at NGFG). These actions show how possible it is to express solidarity with the Palestinian people, and are a good example to follow.

#4087. Roblox users have made a playable version of Counter-Strike and full, working PlayStation games that you can play right now

Multiple remakes of beloved games including Counter Strike, The Simpsons: Hit and Run, and Super Hot, are available to play on Roblox right now. These have not been uploaded by the original game's creators.

One game - which is listed as an 'experience' in Roblox parlance, has been released by Roblox user Takeoff Interactive and listed as 'just a passion project', is a game "inspired by Counter-Strike" and has no monetisation according to its description. Eurogamer played this game today, and it looks and plays exactly like Counter-Strike.

The game includes the standard bomb diffusion mode, where two teams fight over two bomb sites. There are missing sound effects, the smoke doesn't look as good, and a friendly bot stabbed me in the back while diffusing a bomb, but otherwise it looks to be a largely identical recreation of Valve's game, albeit without Valve's involvement.

As for the PlayStation Experience, it's a full working PlayStation 4 dashboard with a media gallery, web browser, and trophies. There's even a server-based chat feature, in which Roblox players can talk to each other. The dashboard includes seven playable games - most of which are indie games. These include: The Simpsons Hit and Run, Cluster Truck, Superhot, Gang Beasts, Five Nights at Freddy's, Undertale, and PaRappaTheRapper.

Eurogamer played The Simpsons Hit and Run, and likewise found it to be a largely identical recreation of Activision's game. Players can drive around Springfield and cause mayhem much like the original game, albeit with a slightly dodgy objective guidance arrow.

Eurogamer also played Superhot, which once again looks and plays much like the original game, though it's not quite as visually impressive. This version of Superhot, Simpsons Hit and Run, and the PlayStation Experience as a whole was uploaded to Roblox by user Redwing Works, not Activision, not the Superhot team, and not Sony.

It is worth noting these are not Roblox games that are merely inspired by popular releases outside its ecosystem. Previously, a few popular Roblox games inspired by the game but not openly copying it exist. Counter Blox, for example, is a tactical FPS which uses Roblox assets and models, while Arsenal is another FPS inspired by Counter-Strike's Gun Game mode in which each kill progresses you to different weapons.

This is not the first time a popular game has been recreated on Roblox without the permission of its creators. The Peak developers urged people to pirate their game rather than play a "microtransaction-riddled ripoff slop" on Roblox.

Eurogamer has contacted Sony and developers for comment.

The Switch 2 is still comfortably ahead of the Switch in its first year, but it might not be ahead by its second.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Switch 2 sales have plummeted over the summer months compared to this time last year; accounting for a drop of nearly four million units. That's sure to be a warning sign for Nintendo, especially as the company increased the price for the handheld across the globe at the start of September—near the end of the period it's currently reporting—which could have an impact on future sales over the busy holiday period.

Nintendo has reported its sales figures from April 1, 2026 until September 30, 2026. It calls this period 'FY27 Q1-Q2' because companies are weird. Nevertheless, it's the previous six months of the year, and it's been a tough one for hardware.

The Switch 2 sold 6.49 million units: a 3.87 million unit reduction compared to the 10.36 million in the same period last year. That makes a change from the original Switch, which sold in increasingly larger amounts for the first five years of its life.

The Switch sold just 1.27 million units during the same period, down 32.7%, but that's not a huge surprise for the outgoing handheld.

So, what to make of the dip? It is a marked reduction in Switch 2 sales compared to its bumper launch year. But that's the thing. The Switch 2 sold incredibly well in its first year; 19.8 million units sold. That's a bigger success story than the Switch. It launched just before the end of Nintendo's weird financial years but reached around 17.7 million units sold by the end of its first full year. Though it did go on to double that figure the following year, which the Switch 2 is likely to fail to achieve.

Nintendo raised the price of the Switch 2 over the course of this summer period. It first announced the price increase in May, 2026; however, it didn't implement it until September 1, 2026 in most of the affected regions (US, Canada, Europe). Only Japan saw a sudden price increase effective in May, 2026.

The company asks $500 for the console, an increase of $50 over its original launch price. It blamed "changes in market conditions" at the time, which is common parlance for 'memory prices are ruining everything.'

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The most recent reporting period ended on September 30. So we don't quite know what impact that $50 price hike will have on the success of the handheld from these figures alone; however, Nintendo has reevaluated its forecast up until March 31, 2027 at just 16.5 million Switch 2 units sold; down from 19.86 million in the previous 12-month period. That's a 16.9% reduction.

"Although unit sales of Nintendo Switch 2 hardware declined compared to the same period of last fiscal year, many consumers continued to adopt the system, spurred on by factors like the release of new titles," Nintendo says.

And it's true, games are flying off the shelves for the Switch 2 relative to last year. Up 18.8%, from 20.62 million to 24.49 million. A certain remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time might help bump those figures, with the game coming out today. Even Switch titles are selling like hot cakes; the majority of game sales remain with the bulk of players on the last-gen console. Up 6.8%, from 61.56 million to 65.73 million.

So it's not all bad for Nintendo—it still has one of the best-selling consoles on its hands. It's just been curtailed by the pesky memory and cost of living crises. Haven't we all?

As Xbox's execs continue to pine for game-related announcements to fill in the gaps between their rounds of mass layoffs, The Elder Scrolls 6 is reportedly set to gain the subtitle Sentinel soon. That's according to a report which also includes some details of where the game that's long been a twinkle in the eye of Skyrim's dad will be set and what its plot will involve.

According to The Verge, The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel could be getting some sort of re-reveal in November that'll lock that in as its full title. Skyrim turns 15 on November 11th, so if Bethesda are looking for a date with some TES significance to it, that one would fit the bill.

Beyond the name, the report points to Hammerfell as the game's setting, something the aforementioned name being confirmed would make obvious if you're an Elder Scrolls nerd like me and know that Sentinel is the name of both a kingdom and city in the Redguards' province. As far as I recall, Hammerfell's also been the setting a majority of fans have believed most likely since that infamous TES 6 teaser in 2018, with some thinking a bit of nearby province and Daggerfall setting High Rock might also be included if the game's map spans the Iliac Bay region.

For now, it's deserty Hammerfell, baby. As for what you'll reportedly be up to there, the report points to The Emma Stones 6 having some secrets to explore linked to the mysterious provenance of the Elder Scrolls themselves. Yep, that's the magic bits of paper which blind people by slamming dangerous and unknowable knowledge into their brains, and can also be used for handy tasks like learning the shout needed to defeat Alduin. You're usually lugging a couple around by the time you've finished TES V, no doubt stuffed between cheese wheels in your massive backpack.

All in all, nothing I can see seems to suggest The Elder Scrolls 6 will deviate much from the sort of adventure Skyrim seemed to be teeing up, with the Thalmor-led Aldmeri Dominion on the march to conquer Tamriel and possibly get up to some metaphysical bollocks to return the land to a state resembling a previous era when elves were on top, if theories long-discussed among fans turn out not to be bunkum.

Such a setup would mirror what Skyrim co-lead designer Kurt Kuhlmann outlined earlier this year as the starting point for the direction he might've taken the game, if he'd helmed it rather than departing Bethesda in 2023.

To be honest, the only thing - aside from the Microsoft stink the game can't escape - that's giving me pause in getting too excited about the direction TES 6 seems to be headed in is that fact that the series' world has been left standing still for so long following Skyrim. I'm not saying it needs a reboot, but I am concerned that - ironically given the Elder Scrolls themselves are time-centric artifacts - this might feel like a game a bit out of time unless it can take a big step mechanically.

Experts from across the world of the trading card game give essential tips

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Unless you’ve been living under a Geodude for the last five years, you’ll have probably noticed that Pokémon cards are everywhere. Yet while fans are scrambling to collect full arts and crypto bros are inexplicably treating new sets like lucrative investments, many seem to have forgotten that these beloved bits of paper were actually made to be played with. The question is, then, how do you begin to build a deck?

While you may have memories of being humiliated by a chocolate-coated Charizard back in the school playground, Pokémon TCG has come a long way since the '00s. Boasting over 1 million dollar prize pools and attracting millions of viewers today, Pokémon cards have slowly become one of the deepest and most popular and best card games on the planet.

Yet, despite Pokémon’s cute and cuddly exterior, taking your first steps into the world of competitive 'mon can be surprisingly intimidating. So, to help you make the jump from crazed card collector to Pokémon master, we picked the brains of the greatest minds in competitive Pokémon TCG. Seeking advice from pro player Drew Stephenson (who finished second place in the 2026 Pokémon Europe International Championships) to esteemed Pokémon World Championship TCG commentators, Joe Bernard and Ross Gilbert, here’s a guide on how to build a super effective battle-ready deck that will set your local TCG night ablaze, getting your IRL Ash Ketchum journey fully underway.

All trainers want to be the very best, and in order to get this TCG train rolling you’ll need a good engine powering your deck. An engine in Pokemon TCG is a set of cards that work together to rapidly draw, search for, or cycle through cards in your deck. So, in other words, before picking your main ‘mon attackers, you need to establish how your deck draws cards and sets up.Ross Gilbert: "Think about your engine first. Don't pick your deck; pick your engine. Once you've picked the engine you're playing, then you can think about what kind of Pokémon to play along with it. The vast majority of the time, the best decks all have a really good engine to draw cards and get rolling."

If you want to build a deck using the most recent cards, Delta Reign just launched. Walmart has the most readily available stock right now, but be aware that artificial inflation and resellers have increased the cost. Meanwhile, UK fans should head straight to Amazon thanks to its 'invite by request' system keeping costs down.

Drew Stephenson: "You've got to think of your deck as an engine... The best thing to look at when you're trying to build a deck is synergy. If I have a card, I want it to also work with another card in my deck. I wouldn't put an Item card in my deck that only searches for one specific Pokémon if it's unlikely I'm going to be able to find it to then get another one. You want it to run well, link in with each other, and function smoothly. If you can make it so your deck always functions smoothly in the games you're playing - whether online or with your friends - that's where you want to be."

We all know that putting together a deck filled with badass Pokémon is the most fun part of deck building, but without trainer cards, you may never even draw the killer ‘mon you’ve built your deck around.

Drew Stephenson: "New players always undervalue Trainer cards. You have limits on what you can do on each of your turns: you can attach one Energy, and you can evolve a Pokémon once each turn. With an Item card, you can play as many as you want during your turn. They're the power cards that dictate the game."Joe Bernard: "The fundamentals of deck building really are: you always want your deck to be functioning in the first place, so you need to have a healthy amount of searching cards, drawing cards, and Trainer cards that just get you into games."

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

Every competitive deck relies on three core types of Trainer cards to stay consistent and interact properly with your opponent. Which specific cards have proven essential throughout recent tournaments? You’ll have to hear it from the pros…Ross Gilbert: "There are three types of cards to think about:

Joe Bernard: "From a raw consistency standpoint, Ultra Ball is so versatile because it can get any type of Pokémon. Lillie's Determination is by far the best Supporter card... and gusting effects like Boss's Orders give you a turn-faster win condition by targeting Pokémon trying to power up."

Drew Stephenson: "The effect of Lillie's Determination is that you play it, shuffle your hand into your deck, and draw eight cards, so you can think of that as being able to get more pieces to build your engine. Having that and Buddy-Buddy Poffin, which searches out your Pokémon, means you can develop your board and really get into playing the game."

Thanks to the prevalence of deck-building websites, many players simply opt to copy common meta decks, or build their decks around countering prevalent meta decks at competitions. These pros argue that instead, you should focus around making a strong and versatile deck that plays well on its own, rather than worrying about a deck that only works against one incredibly specific matchup.Joe Bernard: "Consider covering the weaknesses of your own deck and being aware of what else is being played. There's no point in having a strategy that's really good at beating some decks if those are the decks you're not going to face in a tournament. You need to have your finger on the pulse of what's popular.Simplicity is key. A common trap is to be so focused on one matchup, rather than making your own strategy the problem for someone else to overcome. Whenever you can see clean lists with four counts of the cards you're trying to play, it means you can replicate that strategy much more consistently. Execute your strategy as often as possible."

Learning the basics of a 30 card deck in TCG Pocket is a great place to master the basics, but once you are ready for the full fat physical experience, websites like Limitless TCG let players easily find and build the best decks. Yet where the prevalence of easy to access information should in theory provide a world of deck-building possibilities, instead it has largely driven people to replicate the same proven current meta decks. The pros tips? Be brave, innovate!Drew Stephenson: "With the increase in popularity of the game, and with technology, everyone wants easy access to decks, knowledge, and information. You see a lot of stuff online with winning deck lists - one tournament will happen, and then everyone will be playing against it or playing with it. So there's actually a bit of a lull in creativity in the game right now.

But because of that, since everyone is so used to certain things, having a spark of creativity yourself gives you quite a big advantage. That's why you see a lot of creative decks and spicy strategies doing well right now, and that's personally my favourite part of the game. I've always done well by introducing a bit of creativity into my deck lists."

Ross Gilbert: "I recommend everyone go to Limitless TCG. You can look at individual decks and see how common certain cards are. Net decking is fantastic - grab a list online, copy it, play a bunch, and as you play you can slowly adapt proven decks to your personal playstyle."Want another trading card game with a slightly different pace? Here's how to play Magic: The Gathering.

#4083. "This is a serious incident" - Kingdom Come: Deliverance developer Warhorse suffers cyberattack

Studio working to determine "full extent".

Kingdom Come: Deliverance developer Warhorse Studios has confirmed it's suffered a "serious" cyberattack, saying it is currently working to determine the "full extent" of its impact.

"To our players and friends," a statement by the studio read. "We're sorry to share that Warhorse Studios has been hit by a cyberattack. We're working with cybersecurity specialists to secure our systems and understand the full extent of what happened. Thank you for standing with us." The message was released at 11am GMT and there hasn't been an update from the studio since. We've separately asked the studio if there have been any developments.

Warhorse CEO Martin Frývaldský discussed the incident in a Czech report (translated by DeepL), saying, "This is a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and for everyone affected. Our immediate priority is to secure our systems, determine the full extent of the breach, and take all necessary steps to protect our employees, partners, and our community. We are devoting all necessary resources and capabilities to resolving this situation."

Warhorse is currently working on two games, including a prestigious open-world Middle-earth role-playing game, based on Tolkien's legendary The Lord of the Rings fiction. It's also developing "a new Kingdom Come adventure", which we assume to be Kingdom Come: Deliverance 3. In addition, it's collaborating on a Kingdom Come: Deliverance film.

#4082. DAMON and BABY free update ‘RISE OF THE ORACLE’ announced alongside Switch 2 version

Arc System Works has announced top-down action adventure shooter DAMON and BABY free update “RISE OF THE ORACLE.” It will launch on February 18, 2027 alongside a physical edition of the game for PlayStation 5 and Switch. A digital-only Switch 2 version of DAMON and BABY is also planned for release, which will be available as a free upgrade for Switch owners. A release date was not announced.

The physical edition of DAMON and BABY: RISE OF THE ORACLE, which includes the base game, “RISE OF THE ORACLE,” and further quality-of-life improvements, will be priced at $34.99 / 3,960 yen.

Here is an overview of the game and update, via Arc System Works:

■ Shoot, Dodge, and Anticipate. Gun Action That Packs Satisfying Punches Too

Aim in all directions and weave through gaps in enemy fire—a full-fledged twin-stick shooter that demands precise controls and split-second decision-making.

Each weapon, handgun, machine gun, shotgun, RPG, has different range, ammunition capacity, reload time, and mobility, so that aiming, and choosing the right weapon at the right distance can be the difference between life and death. Make good use of your close-range attacks to continue advancing through enemy lines without running out of ammo.

Each area features a boss with its own unique attack patterns and strategies for defeating them. Read their movements, adjust your equipment and tactics, and use your skills to take them down. For players seeking a challenge, there’s also the high-difficulty challenges, Lord Bloodedge’s Trials, which will test your combat and athletic abilities.

■ Exploration-Based Action Gameplay That Takes You on a Vast World

The intricately designed regions are filled with branching routes, hidden passages, and powerful weapons and charms. Acquiring new abilities will allow you to reach previously inaccessible areas. Even areas you’ve already explored will hold new discoveries.

Combine weapons, skills, rings, charms, and food buffs to create a build that suits your playstyle. Will you overwhelm enemies head-on with high firepower, or dodge attacks and snipe from a distance? Re-evaluating your build depending on the tough enemy and finding the optimal solution is the core of this game.

■ A Strange Partnership Between a Demon Lord and a Child

The protagonist is Damon, a demon lord who can’t be separated from a mysterious child. His adventure to break the curse unfolds in a bleak world reminiscent of 1970s America.

The game also supports offline two-player cooperative play. The second player controls a joyful canine companion, helping to overcome challenges by collecting items and assisting in combat.

■ Includes the Extra Story “RISE OF THE ORACLE.” The Battlefield Is a “Japanese-Style Otherworld”

The packaged version includes the main story plus the extra story “RISE OF THE ORACLE.” A new battle against an enemy awaits in the Japanese-style otherworld “Yomotsu-Hirasaka.”

Damon and his companions had been enjoying a brief, tranquil period of calm.

But one day, their everyday life comes to an abrupt end when an urgent plea arrives: “Please, save the person I owe everything to…”

Determined to protect the peace of his beloved family, Damon steps into the unknown, beyond a mysterious door.

New Region “Yomotsu-Hirasaka” and the Three Sacred Treasures

Beyond the door lies an otherworldly realm of the Orient, fragrant with autumn leaves and drifting scent of sweet osmanthus. A mysterious demon taking the form of Japanese folklore monsters and the barriers of Mars, Mercury and Jupiter stand in your way.

A Japanese-style fantasy battle begins as you gather the “Yata no Kagami” (Mirror of Eight Palms), the “Ame no Murakumo no Tsurugi” (Sword of the Gathering Clouds of Heaven), and the “Yasakani no Magatama” (Eight-Slope Jewel) and challenge yourself to a ritual that will break the rules of the entire universe.

A demon who dreams of becoming the Great Demon King. He helped a mysterious child at the request of an old friend but got cursed and has been unable to be separated from that child since.

A child of unknown origin. She innocently adores Damon, and her smile touches the hearts of all those around him.

An apprentice Onmyoji (exorcist). She accompanies Damon providing support on his journey.

A mysterious being, distinct from demons and angels, and Yugeno Mikoto’s mentor.

They are seeking the “Three Sacred Treasures” in order to escape from “Yomotsu-Hirasaka” (the slope to the underworld).

Yugeno Mikoto’s servant. He will give you useful items in exchange for “MANA.”

DAMON and BABY is available now for PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Switch, and PC via Steam.

#4081. GTA 6 is a massive 210GB download on PlayStation 5

There wasn't really any chance Grand Theft Auto 6 wasn't going to be a big download. Thanks to some new information, though, we now have a hard number.

PlayStation Game Size, which tracks PS Store game releases by poking through its backend, has revealed that GTA 6 has a chonky 210GB download size. While the actual space it's going to occupy on your console's SSD may be smaller, everyone will have to download over 200GB to play Rockstar's latest.

It's unclear whether GTA 6 is going to require a day one patch on top, or if it's already included in the 210GB. Given the interest in the game, the same PS Store sleuths will no doubt return to update us if the file size changes.

GTA 6 is expected to be one of the most dense games ever in sheer content. It has a highly-detailed, massive open-world map featuring a big number of side activities beyond what most contemporary games offer. The cinematic, hours-long story is the other element that contributes to that massive file size.

More broadly, while 210GB is a lot, it's not that much more than some of the biggest games on PS5. Call of Duty, for instance, is famous for its gargantuan file sizes when you have multiple modes installed - though in that case, at least, you're able to selectively uninstall the parts you don't play. This might prove tricky for GTA 6 if / when GTA Online arrives, as most of that is built on single-player content, the same map and so on and may not be easy to separate.

Not too long left now. GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Pre-loading begins 12th November, and hopefully that's enough time for everyone to finish that download.

#4080. Rockstar Games employees have locked in a union vote next month, and it'll take place over Grand Theft Auto 6's release window

A date has been locked in for Rockstar Games employees to vote on whether to recognise their developer union. If successful, it will become the largest recognised union across the entirety of the UK video games industry.

The vote, which runs from the 12th to the 26th November, will give workers at Rockstar Games a chance to decide whether Rockstar will formally acknowledge and negotiate with the Rockstar Game Workers Union on matters involving its employees. These dates notably fall on either side of Grand Theft Auto 6's release date, and shortly after Rockstar's head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg: "we go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union."

This announcement also comes as the legal battle between Rockstar and the Independent Workers of Great Britain union over the alleged unfair firing of over 30 employees. The union argues this was an attempt at union busting, whereas Rockstar stands by its decision to fire them for gross misconduct, pointing to the sharing of confidential information in a union Discord as the reason for the intervention.

This case was meant to have finished already. However, it ran long, resulting in its conclusion being delayed to the 17th and 18th of November.

So it's fair to say, November is a big month for Rockstar and its employees. It's entirely possible that by December, developers at the gaming giant will have both a union representing them and an industry shaking release to celebrate. Fingers crossed.

My kingdom for Sony and FromSoftware to do anything with Bloodborne. There's been no remaster, no PC port, and also no sequel. We do have an excuse for that last one, because apparently bureaucracy is constantly getting in the way.

At least, that's what Shawn Layden, ex-president and CEO of Sony Interactive Entertainment America, suggests on The Trophy Room podcast when asked about why it's been all quiet on the Yharnam front. "Bringing back old games has a certain challenge to it," he starts.

"Can you do something that is not only respectful of the original, but can you recreate the phenomenon?" he ponders, responding to the notion of a Bloodborne remake. After the successful Demon's Souls redux from Japan Studio and Bluepoint Games, people have been hoping for other FromSoftware releases to get the same treatment.

Bloodborne doesn't appear to be a likely candidate from what Layden has to say, nor would a sequel be straightforward. "There's a lot of involved rights associated with it," he explains. "And it's something like that where Sony is in there, and [FromSoftware] is in there, and From's parent company is in there, I think just getting everyone to sign off on everything is probably the biggest challenge there."

Such things are major roadblocks in many creative endeavours. I'm going to guess the fact it was co-developed with Japan Studio is what's causing some of the complications here. The company was unfortunately closed in 2020, leaving its IP or stakes therein wherever.

But that's just speculation. The fact is, Sony likes making money, and Bloodborne would be an easy win, and I suspect if these hurdles didn't exist, we'd have seen activity there by now. Alas, the hunter's dream remains just that for now. Good thing the game is still just as satisfying to replay as it ever was.

#4078. It sounds like you shouldn't expect Destiny 2's campaign unvaulting to be ready until 2028, as Bungie tease their plans for the future of the series

When Bungie announced that they would be ceasing to work on major updates for Destiny 2 earlier this year, it obviously felt like that was the end of that, and any future games were not guaranteed whatsoever. Then last month, they announced that they'll be bringing back all of the shooter's vaulted campaigns, which is obviously a lot of work! Now, in a blog post, the developer has outlined where they're at with this process, offering up a timeline of when to expect the unvaulted campaigns, what will be included with them, and light teases for whatever comes after that.

"Our first pass for unvaulting, available to all players, focuses on getting our campaign slate whole again," head of product Josh Deane explains in the blog post. "We're specifically targeting the activity content of Campaigns, Strikes, and Raids from vaulted expansions. Menagerie holds a special place in our hearts (and we've seen years of community requests for a return), so it will be a part of this pass as well." In practical terms, that means the return of the Red War, Forsaken, Curse of Osiris and Warmind campaigns, strikes, raids and raid lairs from said campaigns, and Menagerie Activity with reprised rewards.

The process for this unvaulting apparently began in June as the team scoped the feasibility of it all, and as of now it's pre-production. Full-on production is expected to start in February 2027 at the latest, but it's worth noting that this is expected to take about 12 months to wrap up. That means you won't be jumping back into any of these beloved expansions until 2028 at least, by the sounds of things.

The team also has "stretch goals" that they're investigating for either the unvaulting launch or sometime after, specifically for things like free roam destinations, seasonal activities from Sundial (season 9) to The Coil (season 32), raid and raid lair weapon updates, and PvP maps.

There are seemingly bigger plans for the game too, with some kind of "celebration" to come beyond Moment of Triumph with "new updates", and something referred to as Destiny 'Legacy'; "Our epic journey started over a decade ago, and the whole experience needs to be served to you all where you play today. Expect more information when we come back to you all early next year." Certainly sounds like they're talking about the original Destiny here, but I suppose we should take that with a pinch of salt. Lastly, they mention "Redacted," which is accompanied by this line, "Launch Ventrilo Message: 'We’re back'". No idea what that means, I'll leave that to you Destiny-heads.

Essentially, the core message seems to be that Bungie are "building a new future for Destiny," so, it's not totally dead in the water. You can expect the next major comms update from Bungie in February, too.

"Perhaps this is more a signal that the game could support more player types."

Arc Raiders recently ended its first-ever test for a dedicated PvE mode, following months of player requests. While feedback has generally been favourable, developer Embark has gone quiet about whether the mode will return as a permanent addition.

There's a reason for that: Embark doesn't appear to have made a decision internally. Speaking to MP1st, executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said the team is currently looking through the data and there are several factors to consider.

"Now that we've concluded the PvE matchmaking toggle test, we're doing a deep dive into what that means," said Grøndal. "Of course, we were a bit skeptical about bringing such a mode to the game for historical reasons, but now we need to discuss what we want to do going forward."

The "historical reasons" Grøndal is likely referring to is the fact Arc Raiders started out as a purely PvE co-op shooter, before Embark pivoted during development and created the extraction PvPvE shooter we know today.

Since Arc Raiders' release, however, two different audiences emerged: players who love the uncertainty and higher stakes excitement PvP creates, and those who simply want to engage with the game's deep PvE mechanics without having to worry about other players.

"I think the game has an appeal in its nature and that a certain player type wants to play the game without the stress, you know? Perhaps this is more a signal that the game could support more player types, and we need to figure out how to support that," he explained.

The challenge, according to Grøndal, is creating something that caters to the two different groups of players "without undermining the premise of the game itself". To do that, Embark needs to find the PvE mode's true purpose.

"We need to understand what the need is here," Grøndal explained. "Is it more a chill side mode you can play between more intense PvPvE rounds? Is it more a challenge mode that you can test your skills against AI? Or perhaps it's a full experience with PvE only?"

Indeed, Grøndal previously said that offering two distinct modes for Arc Raiders' different audiences is a possible future for the game, so all options are seemingly being considered, even if the developer can't offer a concrete answer today. "All options will have different implications on how we build future game updates," Grøndal added.

Arc Raiders recently released its biggest update, Frozen Trail, which saw player numbers shoot up to highs the extraction shooter hasn't witnessed in six months.

#4075. After the rough start that was last year's entry, Football Manager 27 is looking to bring you in with a few free days of play before the game's even out

Football Manager 27 is still a good week and ahead out from launch, but if you're quick you can already get to playing it. That's because developer Sports Interactive have released a Launch Preview version of the game that lets you take it for a kickabout before it comes out in earnest.

As the devs explain in a Steam blog post, "running for the next five days, the FM27 Launch Preview will be freely playable," across all of its release platforms. "There’s no additional sign-up required, simply download from your preferred platform and begin turning your football vision into dugout decisions. This is your chance to get hands-on with the complete FM27 experience across all game modes, including Shuffle Draft, the fast-paced new multiplayer addition."

One caveat worth noting is that there may be some bugs or glitches in the game that the devs "will work to address in future updates." This, understandably, may be a touchy subject for some. It didn't exactly have a stellar launch, with early patches having to fix hundreds of bugs and other issues. Not that Steam reviews are the be all, end all, but the game is still sitting at a mostly negative a year on. It's very well possible that getting the new one in folks' hands early is a way to bring back some of the audience they may have lost last year.

Still, it doesn't sound like Football Manager 26 was all bad. Phil spent a lofty 227 hours on the game around when it launched, writing for RPS at the time, "That massive database of players, staff and clubs, layered so expertly over time with systems that make them all feel alive and dynamic, is still thrilling. It’s not a new feature by any stretch, but it feels overly punitive to discount it because the menus are bad and it chugs along whenever you press continue. It’s a bad version of a fundamentally great experience, and that means my brain’s going to be full of AS Roma matters for the foreseeable, no matter how many AI gravestones I see in my feed decrying the death of the series."

#4074. As Skydance merges with Warner Bros. and Paramount, the company offers voluntary redundancy and mandates return to the office

Skydance - the newly formed corporate megazord combining Warner Bros and Paramount - has issued a full five-day return-to-office mandate to employees, and offered voluntary buyouts as the merging of the companies begins.

The company was formed earlier this month following a much-debated $110bn Paramount acquisition of Warner Bros., in which both companies were squished together to be led by a refreshed board, which includes former UK prime minister Tony Blair (in an advisory role), philanthropist Laurene Powell, and former Activision CEO Bobby Kotick.

In an internal email seen by Vertical Slice, CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told employees that in-person collaboration is "vital" for the company going forward.

"Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems," the email read. "Being together isn't just about showing up. It's about inspiring one another, learning and coaching, forming friendships and having access to the casual conversations that spark something great.

"With that in mind, we will adopt a five-day in-office policy across all of Skydance. We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We've seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them."

The voluntary buyouts, meanwhile - which for those who don't know is an opportunity for employees to leave the company with a severance package - were described as a "one time offer", though it was not clear which teams within Skydance are eligible to accept it.

Skydance now includes the gaming studios once under Paramount and Warner Bros. This includes the game studios Netherrealm (Mortal Kombat), Portkey Games (Hogwarts Legacy), Avalanche Software (not to be confused with Avalanche Studios), Paramount Games Studios, and various other WB studios. It is unclear whether developers at these studios have been offered the voluntary buyout, nor when their employees will have to return to the office.

Skydance is not the only company to have offered voluntary buyouts recently. This week Microsoft offered 60,000 of its employees the same deal - that's roughly 25 percent of its staff - amid sweeping Xbox layoffs and its big AI push. Last year, EA also introduced a return-to-office policy to its employees, with its CEO saying in-person work creates "a kinetic energy that fuels creativity."
